source.title: How much data do you need? Part 2: Predicting DL class specific training dataset sizes

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table and equation formatting is imperfect, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies learning-curve fitting to image-classification models, an additional modality, and reports test-set accuracy fit results. It does not test language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal language-model allocations.
record.gate_note: The study's own CIFAR10 experiments compare several fitted curve forms using held-out test accuracy. Its EMNIST experiment selects an arctan model rather than fitting a power law; its reported EMNIST fit result is retained only as evidence about fitting choices, not as a direct power-law result. The discussion of language-model scaling and other cited studies is background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: On CIFAR10 with Resnet18, the study fits a power law of total training-set size plus epoch to test accuracy and compares it with arctan alternatives on the same data (Table 1). This is a weak, new-setting result on whether the power-law form fits image-classification learning curves (V5), and on whether curve form matters (V7). The test is limited: the measure is accuracy, not loss; data size spans only about one order of magnitude (5k–45k); and epoch enters linearly inside the power law. Power-law fitting is a tool here, not the paper's main question. The paper is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that predicting performance from per-class training counts, rather than total dataset size alone, is more accurate and more informative; on CIFAR10 the class-wise arctan model (1) fits best. The cost is many more training runs, so the approach suits cases where labeling is costly relative to training. They draw no conclusion about the validity of power laws as such.
record.recipe_differences: This is an image-classification data-size study using accuracy and class-specific sample counts, not language-model pretraining loss or compute scaling. It compares power-law and other curve forms and also uses class-wise features and epoch count.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit formulation and dataset matter: the full arctan model fits CIFAR10 test accuracy better than the total-dataset-size power-law model, while the EMNIST experiment uses arctan with forward feature selection.

fits_no_version.finding: Individual class counts carry different weight in predicting accuracy. On CIFAR10, truck and ship have the largest arctan coefficients. On EMNIST, class-pair interactions such as 7 and J are selected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning curves depend on per-class data composition, not only on total dataset size.

record.problems: The evidence concerns image-classification accuracy rather than language-model loss. The reported CIFAR10 model comparisons use fit R2 values, and the EMNIST section does not fit or report a power-law model. The paper reports no uncertainty for these fit metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for training-set fit metrics or figure-only prediction plots; Table 1 reports the test-set fit R2 values used here. The EMNIST arctan result is included only for V7, not as a power-law test.

untested.parts: No language models and no pretraining loss; no parameter or compute scaling.
No extrapolation across orders of magnitude. The forward-testing plots are figure-only and cover image accuracy within one order of magnitude.
Not tested: no depth or width comparison.
Loss is not measured; model-size scaling is not tested; video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Only data-size scaling of accuracy over about one decade is covered.
Not tested: no downstream tasks related to scale or pretraining loss.
Exponent dependence on setup, parameter counting, schedule or compute-optimal split is not tested; only fit quality across functional forms is compared.

missing.what: Forward-testing prediction plots for each fitted form, which could bear on in-range predictive accuracy of power-law vs arctan fits. They are figure-only and unreadable in the text.
Fitted power-law parameters for model (2) (a=0.27, b=0.50, c=0.53; total n 0.96, epoch 0.26), giving the exponent in this setting.

record.verdict_notes: The prose says 'the r2 of model (2) is about 8 to 9 % better', which is evidently a typo for model (1), per Table 1. The figure captions call all four CIFAR10 models 'powerlaw function 0–3', although models 1 and 3 use arctan effects. No uncertainty is reported for any fit metric. Treat this as weak evidence: an accuracy-based, small-range, data-only learning-curve study whose aim is per-class data planning.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy losses are measured.
No extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs is tested.
No fixed-compute language-model allocation or parameter/token scaling trend is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or architecture at a fixed parameter count.

The image-classification experiments measure accuracy rather than language-model loss. Video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested; the EMNIST experiment does not fit a power-law model.
The study does not relate downstream-task performance to model scale or pretraining loss.
The study compares fit forms for image-classification accuracy, but does not test language-model exponents, parameter-count conventions, or compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: Resnet18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; up to 195 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Fit the full linear model using individual CIFAR10 class counts and epoch, then evaluate predicted test accuracy.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a competing fitted form; it is not the total-dataset-size power-law model.
rows.check: This power law takes a linear combination of class counts and epoch, not total n, so it is not the standard form. Its test R2 of 87.0% is clearly below the class-wise arctan fit (96.1%). It bears on V5 only as a power-law variant.

rows.subject: Resnet18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; up to 195 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Fit the full arctan model using individual CIFAR10 class counts and epoch, then evaluate predicted test accuracy.
rows.note: This alternative fit performs best in the study, but the row does not itself measure whether a power law holds.
rows.check: This is an arctan comparator, not a power-law fit, so it should not link to V5. For V7 it shows a non-power-law (saturating) form fits much better than the power-law variant r1 (96.1% vs 87.0% test R2). Part of that gain comes from class-wise inputs, not only the functional form.

rows.subject: Resnet18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; up to 195 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Fit the total-dataset-size and epoch model identified in the prose as the standard power-law model (2), then evaluate predicted test accuracy.

conditions.value: totaln model (2); Table 1 calls it totaln linear model

rows.note: The paper identifies model (2) in the prose as its standard power-law fit, though the table describes the formulation as a totaln linear model. Its test accuracy R2 is lower than the full arctan model's 96.1%.
rows.check: Table 1 labels this 'totaln linear model', but the prose calls it the standard power-law model (2). Epoch is added linearly inside the power law. A test R2 of 86.4% is a moderate fit, and the range is about one order of magnitude. No baseline is given; r4 (same inputs, arctan form) is the natural comparator.

rows.subject: Resnet18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; up to 195 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Fit the total-dataset-size and epoch arctan model, then evaluate predicted test accuracy.
rows.note: This competing fit is reported separately; the value alone does not establish the power-law claim.
rows.check: This is an arctan comparator with the same inputs as r3, so it should not link to V5. It fits only slightly better than the power law (88.9% vs 86.4%), so the evidence that functional form matters is weak when inputs are held equal.

rows.subject: mobilenet_v3_large
rows.operation_detail: Fit an arctan model by forward selection using class counts, total training size, epoch, and two-factor interactions.
rows.note: The authors chose arctan rather than power law for EMNIST because of the accuracy distribution; this result is not a power-law fit.
rows.check: This is a forward-selected arctan fit on EMNIST, and no power law was fitted. The authors chose arctan a priori because the accuracy distribution was bimodal. The R2 of 0.987 is a model-selection value, not a test of any version.

relationships.condition: CIFAR10, Resnet18, test accuracy vs training-set size (5k–45k) and epoch
relationships.reason: The power-law fits reach only moderate test R2 (86.4% and 87.0%) over about one decade of data, and saturating arctan forms fit better (r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Power-law test R² reached 86.4% and 87.0% over about one decade of data, while saturating arctan forms fit better.

relationships.condition: CIFAR10, Resnet18, comparison of fitted curve forms
relationships.reason: Fit quality depends on the chosen form. Arctan beats the power law with the same inputs (88.9% vs 86.4%, r3 vs r4), and clearly with class-wise inputs (96.1% vs 87.0%, r1 vs r2). Exponent variation is not examined.
relationships.display_finding: Arctan fit quality exceeds power-law fit quality at 88.9% versus 86.4% with the same inputs and 96.1% versus 87.0% with class-wise inputs.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The total-dataset-size model identified as power law has test accuracy R2 86.4%, while a class-specific arctan fit reaches 96.1%; this is evidence that the power-law form is not uniformly the best fit in this image setting (r2, r3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR10 fitted forms and EMNIST fitting approach
reader_labels.reason: Fit results differ by formulation on CIFAR10, and the study selects an arctan forward-selected model rather than a power law for EMNIST (r1-r5).
